title: Melting Ice
objective: After this level you can explain how warming changes polar seas.
summary: September Arctic ice is shrinking about 12% per decade; the IPCC finds human influence the main driver. Antarctic ice had no clear trend, then record lows. Less ice means more heat and less habitat.

cards.headline: The 20 smallest Arctic ice minimums on record all came in the last 20 years.
cards.body: NSIDC said so in September 2026: every year from 2007 to 2026. Here's how the polar seas are changing, and why it matters to what lives there.

cards.fact: September Arctic sea ice is shrinking by about 12% per decade.
cards.context: Satellites have measured it since 1979, compared with the 1981-2010 average. NASA puts the rate at 12.2% per decade; NSIDC's September 2026 analysis puts it at 11.8% for 1979-2026. The record low still belongs to 2012. Some years dip less than others, but the trend points one way.

cards.headline: What the IPCC concluded
cards.body: In its 2021 report, the IPCC found human influence very likely the main driver of the Arctic's sea ice loss: about 40% less in September between 1979-1988 and 2010-2019. It projects the Arctic is likely to be practically ice-free in September at least once before 2050, in all five scenarios it considered.

cards.headline: The south is different
cards.body: Antarctic sea ice has told a different story. The IPCC found no significant trend from 1979 to 2020, because different regions changed in opposite directions. Then in 2023, the Antarctic winter maximum was the lowest in the satellite record, more than a million square km below the previous record. The IPCC has low confidence in how Antarctic sea ice will change.

cards.headline: Less ice, more heat, fewer homes
cards.body: Losing ice feeds itself. Sea ice reflects 50 to 70% of sunlight; open ocean reflects only about 6% and absorbs the rest, so the water warms and more ice melts. For animals, the ice is home. Loss of sea ice and its snow is the main threat to Level 77's ringed seals, and scientists warn that ice decline could affect Level 75's krill.

mascot.line: White ice bounces sunlight away; dark water soaks it up. That one swap drives a lot of this story.

questions.prompt: Satellites since 1979 show September Arctic sea ice shrinking at about what rate?

options.label: About 1% per decade
options.rationale: Far too slow: it is about 12%.

options.label: About 50% per decade
options.rationale: Far too fast: it is about 12%.

options.label: It has not changed
options.rationale: The 20 smallest minimums all came from 2007 to 2026.

questions.explanation: NASA puts the September decline at 12.2% per decade and NSIDC (2026) at 11.8%: about 12%.

questions.prompt: What did the IPCC find about Antarctic sea ice from 1979 to 2020?

options.label: It shrank faster than the Arctic's
options.rationale: It showed no significant trend overall.

options.label: It grew steadily every single year
options.rationale: Regions changed in opposite directions, with no overall trend.

options.label: It melted away completely every summer
options.rationale: It shrinks in summer but has never vanished.

questions.explanation: The IPCC found no significant trend from 1979 to 2020 because regions changed in opposite directions; record lows came in 2023.

questions.prompt: From Level 36, water can soak up a lot of heat. What happens to sunlight when sea ice gives way to open ocean?

options.label: The water reflects even more of it
It passes straight through to the sea floor
options.rationale: Open water absorbs most of it and warms.

options.label: The water absorbs most of it, and warms
It helps new ice form faster
options.rationale: Absorbed sunlight warms the water, so more ice melts.

questions.explanation: Open ocean reflects only about 6% of sunlight and absorbs the rest, so the water warms and more ice melts.
